\item[Toolchain] The compiler, the linker, and the runtime library.
\item[Sanitizer] An instrumentation pass that reports memory faults.

Each backend supplies its own lowering rules. The toolchain selects the
backend from the target suffix, so the same source tree builds for more

\section{Convergence Rate}

The learning rate $\alpha$ controls the step size. A large $\alpha$
gives a fast first pass, but the loss then oscillates near the minimum.
A small $\alpha$ is stable and needs many more epochs.

The momentum term $\beta$ smooths the gradient estimate over a window
of steps. We keep $\beta = 0.9$ for every run in this report, because a
sweep over \beta changed the final loss by less than one percent.

The decay $\gamma$ is applied once per epoch. In the tuned run the
product of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ after forty epochs is small enough
that the weights stop moving, and we report the loss at that point.

Table~\ref{tab:rates} lists every value.

\section{Notation}

We use a subscript for the layer index and a superscript for the step
index. In every formula below the layer index is $\ell$ and the step
index is $t$.

The hidden state of layer two at step three is written $h_2^3$. The
same quantity for the first layer is $h_1^3$. When the step index is
not important we drop it and write $h_2$ only.

The running text needs the same symbols. The vector h_2 is the state
of layer two. The reader must not confuse it with the weight matrix
$W_2$, which does not change with the step index.

The gradient of the loss with respect to $W_2$ is written $g_2$, and
the accumulated gradient over one epoch is $\hat{g}_2$.

artifact:
\section{Error Model}

The sensor reports a value with additive noise. We model the noise as a
normal variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The
mean $\mu$ is the calibration offset, and the standard deviation
$\sigma$ comes from the data sheet of the part.

A reading of $r$ therefore gives an estimate $r - \mu$ of the true
value. The estimate is unbiased because the noise has mean zero after
the offset is removed. The variance of the estimate is $\sigma^2$, and
the variance of the mean of $n$ readings is $\sigma^2 / n.

The calibration step measures $\mu$ with a reference source. We repeat
the step once per week, because the offset drifts with temperature.

artifact:
\section{Gradient of the Loss}

The training step needs the partial derivative of the loss with respect
to each weight. For the last layer the derivative is
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$, which the chain rule expands into the
product of two terms.

The first term is $\frac{\partial L}$ and the second term
is $\frac{\partial y}{\partial w}$. Both terms are available from the
forward pass, so the backward pass costs about the same as the forward
pass.

For the hidden layers the expansion repeats once per layer. The cost of
the whole backward pass is therefore linear in the depth.

\section{Build Targets}

The build system chains modifiers with dots. The default target is
\verb|make compile|, which builds in the debug mode.

A release build is \verb|make compile.release. The suffix selects the
mode, and a second suffix selects the toolchain, as in
\verb|make compile.release.llvm|.

The test target follows the same rule, so \verb|make test.ttnn| runs
the suite against one backend only. The clean target takes no suffix.

Every artifact lands under \verb|build/<config>/|, where the
configuration name repeats the suffixes in the order above.

\section{Regularized Objective}

The objective adds a penalty on the size of the weights to the mean of
the per-sample losses. The penalty keeps the solution stable when the
number of samples is small.

\begin{displaymath}
J = \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \ell_i \right)
  + \lambda \left[ \frac{1}{2} \sum_j w_j^2
\end{displaymath}

The constant $\lambda$ sets the weight of the penalty. A value of zero
gives the plain mean loss, and a large value drives every weight to
zero.

We select $\lambda$ on the validation split and then refit on the whole
training split with the selected value.

\section{Balance Equations}

The three equations below describe the steady state of the queue. The
arrival rate is $\lambda$ and the service rate is $\mu$.

\begin{align}
p_0 (\lambda) &= p_1 \mu \\
p_1 (\lambda + \mu) &= p_0 \lambda + p_2 \mu \\
p_2 (\mu) &= p_1 \lambda
\end{align}

The sum of the three probabilities is one, which closes the system. The
solution gives the mean queue length as a ratio of the two rates.

A queue with more than three states follows the same pattern, and the
solution is a geometric series in the ratio $\lambda / \mu$.
